title: Aaron and His Sons Ordained as Priests
summary: Before the whole congregation, Moses carries out the ordination God commanded in Exodus 29. He washes Aaron and his sons, dresses Aaron in the high priest's garments, anoints the tabernacle, the altar, and Aaron, and offers a sin offering, a burnt offering, and a ram of ordination, whose blood he puts on the right ear, thumb, and big toe of each priest. The new priests must then stay at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting for seven days until their ordination is complete.
story: Leviticus now turns from law to story. The offerings of chapters 1 to 7 need priests, and chapter 8 installs them, carrying out word for word the instructions God gave in Exodus 29. The pattern is familiar from Exodus, where God first commands the tabernacle (Exodus 25-31) and Israel then builds it exactly as commanded (Exodus 35-40). Here the command becomes an event. The man at the center has a history. Aaron made the golden calf while Moses was on the mountain (Exodus 32), and Deuteronomy 9:20 says the LORD was angry enough to destroy him until Moses prayed for him. Now Moses washes him, clothes him, and anoints him. Chapters 8 to 10 form a single story: the ordination (chapter 8), the first day of service when God's glory appears (chapter 9), and the death of two of Aaron's sons on that same day (chapter 10). Near the end of the wilderness years, Moses will strip these garments from Aaron on Mount Hor and put them on his son Eleazar before Aaron dies (Numbers 20:28).
historical:
This chapter founds the priesthood that served Israel's sanctuary for the rest of its history. The high priesthood passed from Aaron to his son Eleazar and his grandson Phinehas, and under Solomon it settled in the family of Zadok, which held it for centuries. After the exile the high priest became the leading figure in Judea, and the office lasted until the Romans destroyed the temple in AD 70. The ritual described here was the charter for all of it.

Some of the objects in the chapter remain mysterious. The Urim and Thummim placed in the breastpiece (verse 8) were used to seek God's decision in hard cases (Numbers 27:21), probably as some form of sacred lot that gave a yes or no answer, though their appearance and use are not described. By the time of the return from exile they had been lost, and the governor ruled that certain priests could not eat the most holy food “until there was a priest to consult the Urim and Thummim” (Ezra 2:63). The gold plate on the turban was engraved with the words “HOLY TO THE LORD” (Exodus 28:36). Anointing with oil to set apart kings and officials was known across the ancient Near East, and in Israel it would later mark kings and, in one case, a prophet (1 Kings 19:16).
cultural:
Every step dramatizes a change of status. Washing removes the ordinary. Clothing gives the office its visible form: tunic, sash, robe, the ephod, and the breastpiece with its twelve stones bearing the names of Israel's tribes, so that Aaron carried the people “over his heart” whenever he entered the Holy Place (Exodus 28:29). Anointing with fragrant oil marks the tabernacle, the altar, and the high priest as belonging to God. Psalm 133 remembers the scene, describing oil running down on the beard, “running down Aaron’s beard over the collar of his robes” (Psalm 133:2).

The blood of the ordination ram touches the right earlobe, the right thumb, and the right big toe. Interpreters have long seen the extremities as standing for the whole person, and the right side as the side of honor and strength. Many add that the ear is for hearing God's word, the hand for doing his work, and the foot for walking in his ways, a reading that suits the rite even if the text does not spell it out. The same three points are marked on a person cleansed from skin disease (14:14), linking the priest being set apart with the outcast being brought back. The Hebrew phrase for ordaining a priest is to fill his hand, possibly from placing portions of the offering in his hands, as Moses does in verse 27.
literary: The chapter is narrative built on a refrain. Again and again it notes that Moses acted as the LORD had commanded him (verses 4, 9, 13, 17, 21, and 29), and it ends with Aaron and his sons doing everything the LORD commanded through Moses (verse 36). The repetition presents the event as obedience, not improvisation. The order moves from preparation to sacrifice to meal: the assembly gathers (1-5), Moses washes, clothes, and anoints (6-13), then offers the sin offering (14-17), the burnt offering (18-21), and the ordination ram (22-29), sprinkles the priests with oil and blood (30), and gives instructions for eating the meat and keeping the seven days (31-36). Moses serves as priest throughout, as he did when the covenant was sealed with blood in Exodus 24, but his role is to install the priesthood, not to hold it. The number seven recurs: the altar is sprinkled seven times, and the ordination lasts seven days.

outline.t: The congregation assembles at the Tent of Meeting
The bull of the sin offering
The ram of the burnt offering
The ordination meal and the seven days

doctrines.note: Holiness is conferred by God, not achieved by the priests. They are washed, clothed, anointed, and sprinkled by another, and they simply receive. The tabernacle and altar are consecrated in the same way, since everything used in God's service must first be set apart for him.

The verb for anointing (mashach) gives the Hebrew word messiah, the anointed one. Priests and kings were anointed in Israel, and the hope for a coming anointed one grew out of these offices. The ordination of Aaron is one of the places where that vocabulary begins.

Before Aaron and his sons can make atonement for anyone else, atonement must be made for them. They lay their hands on the bull of the sin offering for their own sins (verse 14), and Moses says the whole rite was commanded to make atonement on their behalf (verse 34).

words.note: Millu, ordination, literally filling. It comes from the idiom to fill the hand, which means to install someone in office. The ram of ordination (verse 22) is the offering that completes this filling, and verse 33 says literally that he will fill your hand for seven days. The same idiom is used in Judges 17:5, where Micah installs one of his sons as priest.

Mashach, to anoint, to smear or pour oil on something. Here Moses anoints the tabernacle, its furnishings, and Aaron. The noun formed from it, mashiach, means anointed one and is the source of the word messiah; its Greek equivalent is christos.

Qadash, to consecrate or make holy. It means to set something apart from ordinary use for God's use. Objects, places, times, and people can all be consecrated. The chapter uses it for the tabernacle, the altar, and the priests, all of which now belong to God in a special way.

christ: The New Testament reads this chapter through the figure of Jesus as high priest. Hebrews notes that the office is never self-appointed: “No one takes this honor upon himself; he must be called by God, just as Aaron was” (Hebrews 5:4), and Christ was likewise appointed by God (5:5). It also marks the difference. Aaron needed a sin offering for his own sins before he could serve, but Jesus “does not need to offer daily sacrifices, first for His own sins and then for the sins of the people” (Hebrews 7:27). The title Christ means anointed one, and Jesus applied to himself Isaiah's words, “The Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me” (Luke 4:18). The New Testament also extends priesthood to God's people as a whole, calling believers “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9) and saying that Christ has made us “a kingdom, priests to His God and Father” (Revelation 1:6). Christians differ on how this relates to ordained ministry, but they agree that the priesthood Aaron received pointed beyond itself.

hard.q: Why would God make Aaron, the man who built the golden calf, Israel's high priest?
hard.a:
The difficulty is real. In Exodus 32 Aaron shaped the calf, built an altar before it, and then gave Moses a lame excuse about the calf coming out of the fire by itself (Exodus 32:24). Leviticus 8 does not mention any of this, and nothing in the chapter suggests Aaron earned his office afterward.

The Bible's own answers point in several directions. First, the priesthood rests on God's choice, announced before the calf incident (Exodus 28-29), and God does not withdraw it. Second, Aaron survived only because Moses interceded for him (Deuteronomy 9:20), so his office began in mercy. Third, the ordination itself begins with a sin offering for Aaron and his sons (verse 14), and his first act of service in chapter 9 is to offer a calf for his own sin. The priesthood never pretended that priests were sinless. Hebrews draws out the benefit: a human high priest “is able to deal gently with those who are ignorant and misguided, since he himself is beset by weakness” (Hebrews 5:2). The same book adds that such a priesthood could only point ahead to one who would not need atonement for himself.

questions: Aaron did nothing in this chapter but receive: washing, clothing, anointing. What does that suggest about how people are made fit to serve God?
The blood touched the ear, the hand, and the foot. What would it mean for your hearing, your work, and your daily steps to be set apart for God?
The man who made the golden calf was ordained as high priest. How does God's willingness to use people with failures in their past change the way you see your own history?
